title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
The problem
Code gets shared. Secrets must not.

An API key typed into a script travels with that script — everywhere.

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code

Where a hardcoded key ends up
API_KEY = "sk-abc123yourrealkeyhere"   # never


Git history
Deleting the line later doesn’t help. Old commits keep it.


Shared files
Notebooks, exports, screenshots, screen shares.


Everyone with access
Teammates, forks, and anyone who ever clones the repo.

text:
The fix: separate config from code


Your code
no secret inside

←

Environment
API_KEY=…

←

Where it’s stored
.env file · secret store



The code is identical on every machine
Only the environment changes: laptop, server, Databricks
The secret is never committed

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
What is an environment variable?
A named string the operating system hands to your program.
import os

os.getenv("API_KEY")                       # None if missing
os.environ["API_KEY"]                      # KeyError if missing
os.getenv("API_URL", "http://localhost")   # with a default
Always strings. Convert numbers and booleans yourself.

First, install the package:
pip install python-dotenv

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
1 Write a .env file
One NAME=value per line, in your project folder.


.env

API_KEY=sk-abc123yourrealkeyhere
API_URL=https://api.example.com
DEBUG=true


No spaces around =
Quotes only needed if the value has spaces
# starts a comment

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
2 Keep it out of Git


.gitignore

.env

Then commit a template so teammates know what to set:


.env.example

API_KEY=your-key-here
API_URL=https://api.example.com


Add .env to .gitignore before your first commit.

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
3 Load it in Python
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()                      # .env → os.environ

api_key = os.getenv("API_KEY")
api_url = os.getenv("API_URL")
Call load_dotenv() once, at the top of your entry script.

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
Use it, never print it
import requests

resp = requests.get(
    api_url,
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
)
print(resp.status_code)


200
Key is valid


401 / 403
Key is wrong or expired

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
section: Fail fast when a key is missing
text:
Fail fast when a key is missing
def require(name):
    value = os.getenv(name)
    if not value:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Missing env var: {name}")
    return value

api_key = require("API_KEY")
A clear error at startup beats a confusing 401 ten minutes later.

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
Handy options
load_dotenv(find_dotenv())      # search parent folders
load_dotenv(".env.dev")         # a specific file
load_dotenv(override=True)      # .env wins over real env

config = dotenv_values(".env")  # a dict, os.environ untouched
By default load_dotenv() does not overwrite variables already set. Servers and CI can override your local file.

In the UI

Catalog → your schema → Secrets
Open the secret

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
askpass: type it when needed
# install.packages("askpass")
api_key <- askpass::askpass("Enter your API key")

Pops up a password prompt, typed characters hidden
Returns the value as a string
Nothing is written to disk

Good for quick interactive work. You retype the key each session.

title: Keep Your Secrets Out of Your Code
text:
keyring: store it once
# install.packages("keyring")
keyring::key_set("my-api")          # prompts once, then stores it
api_key <- keyring::key_get("my-api")

Saved in your OS credential store (Keychain, Credential Manager)
Read it back in any script, no file in your project
Closest R equivalent to Databricks secrets

Never put the key itself in your code. Only the name "my-api".

title: Build a Short Training

You’re teaching, not presenting
A presentation ends when you stop talking. A training ends when they can do it.

Every team owes one. Pick something your project needs, and you’ll learn it properly by teaching it.

title: Build a Short Training
text:
The shape of a training


Frame the need

→

Navigate to details

→

Give examples

→

Let them practice

→

Review / reflect




Slides carry the first two steps.

Code carries the next two.

Frame all of it the way industry would: why a team would pay for this skill.

title: Build a Short Training
text:
1 · Frame the need
One slide. Why should anyone in this room care?

What problem does this solve that we currently solve badly, or not at all?
Where does it show up in our project?
What breaks without it?


If you can’t name the need, don’t teach the tool. Nobody remembers a solution to a problem they never felt.

title: Build a Short Training
text:
2 · Navigate to details
Enough background to follow along, and no more.

The two or three ideas they must hold to read your code
The vocabulary, defined once
Where it sits next to what we already know

Resist teaching the whole API. You are not the documentation.

title: Build a Short Training
text:
3 · Give examples
Working code they can read, on data they recognize.

Start with the smallest version that does something real
Show the output, not just the code
Use our C-Store data where you can, so nobody is learning a new dataset at the same time
Build up in steps: one idea per cell

title: Build a Short Training
text:
4 · Let them practice
This is the part teams skip. It’s the part that works.


Make it runnable
A notebook in our GitHub org, or a Databricks notebook they can clone.


Make it small
Ten minutes, with a clear finish line. Not a project.


Make it graded by them
Give the expected output, so they know whether they got it.


Walk the room while they work. Where they get stuck is your real feedback.

title: Build a Short Training
text:
5 · Review and reflect
Close the loop.

What should they be able to do now that they couldn’t before?
The one mistake you’d bet most of them made
Where to look next: docs, a guide, the book chapter

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
The question
What sells with what?

Every rule you find has to survive one question: what would the store do differently tomorrow?

title: Baskets of Goods
section: A basket is a row per transaction
text:
A basket is a row per transaction


Line items
one row per scan

→

Basket
one row per transaction

→

Rules
one row per rule


A basket is the set of categories in one transaction. Duplicates collapse: two energy drinks count as one Packaged Beverages.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
Three numbers describe a rule
For a rule A → B:


Support
How often A and B appear together, out of all baskets.
Is it common enough to care?


Confidence
Of baskets with A, how many also have B.
How reliable is the rule?


Lift
Confidence ÷ how often B shows up anyway.
Does A actually tell us anything?


Lift is the one that matters. High confidence on a very common item means nothing.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
The arithmetic, on our data
Beer → Cigarettes, from the multi-item baskets:




Value
Where it comes from




Support
0.065
6.5% of baskets have both


Confidence
0.318
31.8% of beer baskets also have cigarettes


Cigarettes alone
0.187
18.7% of all baskets have cigarettes


Lift
1.70
0.318 ÷ 0.187



Beer buyers are 1.7× more likely than average to also buy cigarettes.
Example conclusions — one run on the Idaho sample, not a finished analysis.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
Reading lift


Lift > 1
They go together more than chance. Worth acting on.


Lift ≈ 1
Independent. The rule tells you nothing.


Lift < 1
They repel. Buying A makes B less likely.



Association is not causation. A rule says the two co-occur, not that moving one moves the other. That’s what a test or a promotion proves.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
What makes C-Store baskets different


Baskets are tiny
A drink. A pack of cigarettes. Fuel only. Support is low for everything.


A few categories dominate
Fuel, tobacco, lottery, and services swamp the counts.


SKUs are too fine
Hundreds of drink SKUs give sparse, unactionable rules. Roll up to category.


Time and place matter
Morning coffee baskets look nothing like Friday-evening beer baskets.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
Profile first


2.7M line items in the Idaho sample


1.5M baskets, averaging 1.8 items


56% of baskets hold a single item


More than half the data carries no co-occurrence at all. Profile before you mine, or you’ll tune thresholds blind.
Example conclusions — one run on the Idaho sample, not a finished analysis.

title: Baskets of Goods
section: Cleaning: what counts as a basket
text:
Cleaning: what counts as a basket

Single-item baskets: keep them and support collapses; drop them and every number is conditional on “basket had 2+ items.”
Fuel, tobacco, lottery: so common they attach to everything. Tag them, then decide whether they’re items or context.


Every one of these changes your rules. Write the decision down, and report your numbers next to it.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
Roll up to category



At SKU level
20OZ MTN DEW → 44OZ REIGN
Support near zero. Thousands of rules, none actionable.



At category level
Packaged Beverages → Salty Snacks
Enough support to act on. A planogram decision.


The GTIN table gives you CATEGORY, SUBCATEGORY, BRAND, and PRODUCT_TYPE. Start at category, go finer only where a rule earns it.

title: Baskets of Goods
text:
FP-Growth finds the rules
Spark’s FPGrowth does the counting. You give it baskets and two thresholds:


Minimum support
How rare an itemset can be before it’s ignored.
We used 0.5%, not the textbook 1%, because baskets are tiny.


Minimum confidence
How weak a rule can be before it’s dropped.
We used 5%, then sorted by lift.


It builds a tree of frequent items instead of rescanning for every combination, so it scales where the textbook Apriori algorithm stalls.

title: Baskets of Goods
section: One more decision before you mine
text:
One more decision before you mine
We ran it on multi-item baskets only: 211,282 of 886,936.

Keep the single-item baskets and support collapses toward zero.
Drop them and every number becomes “out of baskets that had 2 or more items.”


Neither is wrong, but the denominator changes every result. Say which one you used, every time you report a lift.

Example conclusions — one run on the Idaho sample, not a finished analysis.

silver = silver.withColumn("daypart",
    F.when(F.hour("DATE_TIME") < 10, "morning")
     .when(F.hour("DATE_TIME") < 15, "midday")

section: Why this is the feature-engineering skill
text:
Why this is the feature-engineering skill

Your unit of analysis decides which one you need.
groupBy builds the table: one row per shopper, store, or week.
over(Window) adds context without collapsing: this basket vs. that shopper’s average.
partitionBy + orderBy gives you lags, ranks and running totals — the temporal features.


If you can’t say whether a calculation changes the row count, you don’t know what you’re building yet.

What makes data “big”?



Volume
Size on disk. If it fits and runs on your laptop, it isn’t big. Today, hundreds of GB signals big.



Variety
Many types of data: photos, video, spatial, time series, text. Each needs its own storage and retrieval.



Velocity
How fast data arrives: sensors at thousands of readings a second, card transactions.


Usually two of the three earn the word “big.”

This course focuses on simplified volume and velocity: batch processing toward a predictive model, not streaming or real-time decisions.

Rows or columns?


Row-oriented (CSV)
placekey, region, visits
aaa,      UT,     120
bbb,      GA,     85
ccc,      UT,     240
To sum visits, you read every value in every row.

Column-oriented (Parquet)
placekey: aaa, bbb, ccc
region:   UT,  GA,  UT
visits:   120, 85,  240
To sum visits, you read one column and skip the rest.

title: Data Sizes, Formats, and Tools
text:
What Parquet gives you

Columnar: read only the columns you need.
Compressed: similar values sit together, so they compress well.
Typed schema: numbers stay numbers. Nested lists and structs stay nested.
Statistics: min and max per chunk let tools skip data a filter can’t match.
Open standard: Polars, pandas, DuckDB, Spark, R, and Databricks all read it.

section: Parquet on disk, Arrow in memory
text:
Parquet on disk, Arrow in memory



Apache Parquet
A file format. Compressed and encoded for storage. Built to be small and fast to scan.



Apache Arrow
A memory format. Columnar and uncompressed. Built for fast computation.



disk: .parquet → memory: Arrow columns → Polars · pandas · DuckDB · Spark

title: Data Sizes, Formats, and Tools
text:
Why Arrow matters

One shared layout. Tools that speak Arrow can hand data to each other without copying or converting it.
Polars is built on Arrow. Its DataFrames are Arrow columns.
Spark uses Arrow to move data to and from pandas (toPandas(), pandas UDFs).
Columnar in memory means fast operations on whole columns at once.


Parquet is how data rests. Arrow is how data moves and gets computed.

title: Data Sizes, Formats, and Tools
text:
The same question in both
Total visits to religious buildings by state:

PolarsPySpark


import polars as pl

places = pl.scan_parquet("places.parquet")
patterns = pl.scan_parquet("patterns.parquet")

(places
    .filter(pl.col("top_category") == "Religious Organizations")
    .join(patterns, on="placekey")
    .group_by("region")
    .agg(pl.col("raw_visit_counts").sum().alias("visits"))
    .collect())


from pyspark.sql import functions as F

places = spark.read.parquet("places.parquet")
patterns = spark.read.parquet("patterns.parquet")

(places
    .filter(F.col("top_category") == "Religious Organizations")
    .join(patterns, on="placekey")
    .groupBy("region")
    .agg(F.sum("raw_visit_counts").alias("visits"))
    .show())

title: Data Sizes, Formats, and Tools
text:
Both are lazy
Nothing runs until you ask for a result (.collect() in Polars, .show() in Spark). First, the tool plans the query:
Parquet SCAN [places.parquet]
  PROJECT 3/25 COLUMNS
  SELECTION: col("top_category") == "Religious Organizations"
Parquet SCAN [patterns.parquet]
  PROJECT 2/22 COLUMNS
The planner read 5 of 47 columns and filtered while scanning. That’s Parquet and a lazy engine working together.

title: What to Show on the Pump Screen
text:
The setting
Ninety seconds. One screen. One offer.

The customer is standing at the pump watching the gallons tick. What do you put in front of them, and how did you decide?

title: What to Show on the Pump Screen
section: It’s a decision, not a prediction
text:
It’s a decision, not a prediction
A model that says this shopper has a 23% chance of buying a drink hasn’t decided anything yet.


Predict
How likely is each outcome?


Value it
What is each outcome worth, minus what the offer costs?


Choose
Show the one offer with the highest expected value.


Expected value = P(accepts) × margin − cost of the discount. Every method below is a way to get that first number.

title: What to Show on the Pump Screen
text:
1 · Association rules
“People who buy this also buy that.”



No model to train, no cold start
Works on the first visit, with no shopper ID
Explainable to a store manager in one sentence



The limit
It describes the basket, not the person. Everyone buying fuel sees the same offer.


Reference: Baskets of Goods →

title: What to Show on the Pump Screen
text:
2 · Segment-based offers
Cluster the shoppers, then write one offer per segment.

Stable: segments don’t move week to week
Explainable: morning commuters get coffee, fill-up-only gets a car wash
A human can sanity-check every offer before it ships


The limit
Everyone in a segment gets the same thing, and your segments were built to describe shoppers, not to predict what they’d accept.

Reference: Customer Segmentation →

title: What to Show on the Pump Screen
text:
3 · Propensity models
One model per offer: P(buys this category | what we know at the pump).

Ranks offers by probability for this visit
Uses the features you’ve been building: fuel grade, gallons, daypart, history
Scales to as many candidate offers as you have models


The limit
It predicts what they’d do anyway. Your best-scoring offer is often the thing they were already going to buy.

Reference: Labeled Baskets →

title: What to Show on the Pump Screen
text:
4 · Uplift models
Don’t predict the purchase. Predict the change in purchase.



Persuadable
Buys only if shown the offer. The only group worth paying for.


Sure thing
Buys either way. The discount is pure margin loss.



Lost cause
Never buys. Wasted screen.


Sleeping dog
Buys unless you bother them. Rare, but real.


You need a holdout — some customers get no offer — or you can never measure uplift.

title: What to Show on the Pump Screen
text:
5 · Contextual bandits
Learn while serving. Mostly show the offer you believe is best, and sometimes try another to keep learning.

Handles a changing offer lineup without retraining from scratch
Solves the cold-start problem by exploring
Measures itself as it runs


The limit
Hardest to build, hardest to explain to a client, and it needs real-time serving at the pump.

title: What to Show on the Pump Screen
text:
The honest constraints


29.6% of transactions carry a shopper ID — and it’s card-based


52% of shoppers appear more than once in two years


12.2% of fuel visits include an in-store purchase


Roughly seven in ten visits are anonymous to us. A personalization plan that assumes a known shopper fails most of the time.

Build the anonymous tier first. It covers most visits, needs no identity, and gives you the baseline that everything else has to beat.

The pump screen only knows what you can compute before the customer walks in:

Fuel grade, gallons so far, payment type, pump number

For recognized shoppers: visit count, days since last visit, past mission mix


Anything you can’t know at the moment of the offer is not a feature. That’s the same leakage rule, with a clock on it.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
Where we are
Rules found what sells together. Labels predicted one outcome.

Segmentation asks a different question: who are these customers, and how many kinds are there?

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
Unlabeled learning
There is no Y. No right answer to train against, so nothing to score yourself against at the end.


Supervised
You know the answer for past rows. The model learns to reproduce it.
Did this visit include fuel?


Unsupervised
You have only the features. The model looks for structure.
What kinds of shoppers are there?


That freedom is the danger: an algorithm will always return groups, whether or not they mean anything.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
Clustering

Partitioning a set of objects into groups so that objects in the same group are more similar to each other than to those in other groups.

The analyst defines “similar.” That choice — which features, on what scale — decides the answer more than the algorithm does.

Clusters are a hypothesis, not a finding. You still have to show they’re stable and that someone can act on them.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
k-means vs. HDBSCAN

Illustrative: make_moons and make_blobs from scikit-learn, not customer data.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
What the picture shows



k-means

You must pick k in advance
Cuts by distance to a centre, so it only finds round blobs
Every point gets a cluster, outliers included




HDBSCAN

Finds the number of clusters itself
Follows density, so shapes can be anything
Points in sparse regions are labeled noise, not forced



For customers, “I don’t know how many segments there are” and “some shoppers fit no segment” are both honest, so HDBSCAN fits the problem.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
The two knobs

min_cluster_size — the smallest group you’ll accept as a segment. Larger values are more robust on noisy data.
min_samples — how dense a neighborhood must be for a point to count as core. Higher means more points called noise. Defaults to min_cluster_size; tune it second.

labels = HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=100, min_samples=20).fit_predict(X)
For a customer product, set min_cluster_size to your privacy floor: no segment smaller than the number of shoppers you’re willing to report on.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
The curse of dimensionality
With 20 behavioral features per shopper, distance stops meaning much: in high dimensions, everything is far from everything, and “nearest neighbor” loses its edge over the average point.

Distances concentrate, so density looks flat
Sparse space, so clusters have no room to be dense
Compute cost grows with every column

Dimension reduction maps the data to fewer dimensions while keeping what matters: which points are near which.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
UMAP
Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection.

Find each point’s nearest neighbors in the original high-dimensional space.
Build a graph of those neighbor relationships.
Lay the graph out in 2 to 5 dimensions, nudging points until the layout preserves the neighborhoods.



n_neighbors
Small keeps local detail. Large keeps the global shape.


min_dist
How tightly points may pack. Low for clustering, higher for a readable picture.


n_components
Output dimensions. 5 to cluster, 2 to draw.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
UMAP on handwritten digits

64 pixel columns, projected to 2. HDBSCAN found 12 clusters with 1.8% noise — close to the 10 true digits, splitting a couple of them.
Illustrative: scikit-learn digits, not customer data.

title: Customer Segmentation
section: Why digits are the honest test
text:
Why digits are the honest test
We know the answer here: 10 digits. So we can see the failure modes you won’t see on customers:

Some digits split into two clusters (different handwriting styles)
Some sit next to each other (4, 7 and 9 overlap)
A few points land in no cluster


On customer data nobody hands you the digits. That’s why stability checks replace accuracy.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
The pipeline


1 Features
~20 per shopper

→

2 Scale
log, standardize

→

3 UMAP → 5-D

→

4 HDBSCAN

→

5 Name them
profile each group


Scaling matters more than it looks. Dollars run to the hundreds and trip counts to single digits, so without scaling, spend decides every cluster.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
Features for a C-Store shopper



Frequency and value: trips, basket total, items per trip
Timing: daypart shares, weekday vs. weekend



Mission: fuel, fountain and food, packaged drinks, snacks, tobacco
Price and payment: discount use, credit vs. debit


Leave store brand out of the features. Otherwise you cluster by where people shop, then “discover” that each brand has its own shoppers.

title: Customer Segmentation
section: Pick the unit of analysis first
text:
Pick the unit of analysis first
One row per what? For segments, it’s one row per shopper, not per basket — but over what span?


One week
A trial run split the segments almost entirely by daypart, because most shoppers made a single trip.


A quarter or more
Enough trips per shopper that frequency, mission and timing can vary within a row.


Example conclusions — from a one-store, one-week sample, not a finished analysis.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
Naming the segments
The model returns 0, 1, 2, -1. You turn those into something a client can use:

Profile each cluster against the features that built it.
Find what makes it different from the average, not what’s biggest in it.
Name it for the behavior: Morning commuters, Fill-up only.
Check the name survives a new quarter of data.


-1 is a real answer. “Unsegmented” shoppers are a group too, and often a big one.

title: Customer Segmentation
section: Spark builds the table, not the clusters
text:
Spark builds the table, not the clusters
UMAP and HDBSCAN are single-machine libraries. Spark ML has k-means, bisecting k-means and Gaussian mixtures — no HDBSCAN.


PySpark
millions of lines → one row per shopper

→

One machine
UMAP + HDBSCAN on the shopper table

→

PySpark
join labels back, profile, write Delta


The heavy lifting is the feature build, and that’s the part Spark is for.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
Why the handoff is fine
The transaction data is big. The shopper table isn’t.


Millions
of transaction lines, across stores and quarters. Spark territory.


~100k rows
one per shopper, with ~20 columns. A few MB in memory.


A table that fits in a driver’s memory doesn’t need a cluster to cluster it. Use Spark to get there, then stop.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
In a Databricks notebook
%pip install umap-learn hdbscan

features = spark.table("workspace.cstore.shopper_features")   # built with Spark
pdf = features.toPandas()                                     # Arrow handles the move

labels = hdbscan.HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=50).fit_predict(
    umap.UMAP(n_components=5, min_dist=0.0).fit_transform(X))

%pip install is notebook-scoped: it installs on the driver for this session.
toPandas() moves everything to the driver. Check the row count first.
Serverless compute gives you a modest driver. If it won’t fit, sample.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
How you know it worked
Without a Y, you check stability and usefulness:

Noise share. If 60% is noise, your features or knobs are wrong.
Across random seeds. Do the same shoppers land together each run?
Across time. Does last quarter’s segment still describe the same people?
Against a simple baseline. Does it beat RFM (recency, frequency, monetary) buckets?
The client test. Can someone name an action per segment? If not, it’s decoration.

title: Customer Segmentation
text:
What segmentation can’t do

It won’t tell you why anyone belongs to a group.
It won’t predict what a shopper does next. That’s a labeled model.
It will give you groups even from noise, so a result alone proves nothing.
Segments drift: refit on a schedule and expect the boundaries to move.
